choices.text: Reference it in the job with `${resources.experiments.churn_exp.id}`, which the bundle resolves at deployment
Let the job create a new experiment with a random name on every run and ignore the one the bundle declared
Look the experiment up by its display name in a notebook cell and skip all bundle configuration
Hard-code the ID of the experiment in the job after the first deployment, and deploy twice

stem: A governed table `ml.crm.customer_dim` is fully rewritten every night by a pipeline. It has no event timestamp that describes when a row happened, and it holds no model predictions. The team wants data quality metrics, such as null rates and distributions, tracked for each nightly state of the whole table. Which profile type fits?

choices.text: An inference profile with the customer id as the model id column, so that every customer is profiled as a separate model
No profile at all, because profiles can be attached only to tables that grow by appending rows and never to rewritten tables
A snapshot profile, which processes the complete table at every refresh and records the metrics for the state of the table at that time
A time series profile on the `updated_at` column, with a daily granularity, so that each nightly rewrite becomes a separate time window

stem: A serving endpoint logs requests and responses to an inference table. The request and response columns hold JSON strings with the feature values and the prediction, and true labels arrive later in a separate table. The team wants an inference profile with accuracy and F1 trends. What should the pipeline do before the profile is created?

choices.text: Create a time series profile on the logged table, because inference profiles accept only tables written by batch scoring jobs and never endpoint logs, and it would give the same metrics
Schedule a job that unpacks the JSON into one column per feature and prediction, joins the labels and creates the profile on the resulting Delta table
Export the table to a CSV file in a volume every night, because profiles are able to read only files and cannot read Delta tables
Create the inference profile directly on the logged table and set the prediction column to the response JSON column, which the profile parses automatically

stem: A team creates a time series profile today on an events table that has two years of history, expecting two years of daily metrics. The first refresh finishes, but the dashboard shows only about the last month. No error is reported. What explains this?

choices.text: The daily granularity discards all windows older than the retention period of the metric tables, which is set to 30 days by default in the profile
The profile processes only the files added since the table was last optimized, and the older files are skipped until a full refresh is requested
The dashboard was created by a different user, and Unity Catalog row filters hide the older windows from everyone except the table owner
When a time series or inference profile is created, only the data from the 30 days before its creation is analyzed; new data is processed after that

stem: A 6TB append-only table of clickstream events, with an `event_ts` timestamp, must be profiled for null rates and distribution drift. A first attempt with a snapshot profile is rejected for size. Refresh cost must also stay low as the table grows. Which configuration meets both needs?

choices.text: A time series profile on `event_ts` with change data feed enabled on the table, so that each refresh processes only newly appended data
An inference profile, because it supports larger tables than snapshot and does not require predictions when the label column is omitted
A snapshot profile on a deep clone refreshed monthly, which keeps the profiled table under the limit while the source continues to grow
A snapshot profile with a slicing expression on `event_ts`, so that each slice is smaller than the maximum table size for snapshots

stem: A platform team has already attached a snapshot profile to `ml.churn.scored_customers`. An ML engineer now tries to create an inference profile on the same table through the API to get accuracy trends, and the call fails. The table does have prediction, label, timestamp and model version columns. What is the correct way forward?

choices.text: Delete the snapshot profile, or profile a separate view or table over the same predictions, because a table can have only one profile
Ask for the MANAGE privilege on the catalog, because creating an additional profile on a table needs a privilege higher than the first one
Create the second profile with a different output schema, because the limit applies to each metric-table location and not to the table
Add inference settings to the existing snapshot profile with an update call, because one profile can combine the snapshot and inference types

stem: An ML engineer holds SELECT on `ml.churn.scored_customers`, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its catalog and schema. Creating a data profile on that table through the API still fails with a permission error. The engineer is not a metastore admin. Which additional privilege resolves it?

choices.text: CREATE MODEL on the schema, because every inference profile registers a small monitoring model there while it is created
MANAGE on the catalog, the schema or the table, which completes the privileges that data profiling requires
Membership in the workspace admins group, because profiles can be created on a table only by workspace administrators
MODIFY on the table, because the profile appends its metric rows back into the profiled table as additional partitions

stem: To profile an endpoint's request log, a team defines a materialized view that unpacks the JSON payloads and joins the labels, and attaches a time series profile to that view. As the log grows, every refresh of the profile takes longer, although only one day of new rows arrives each time. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Change data feed is honored only by snapshot profiles, so a time series profile always reprocesses the table; recreate the profile as a snapshot profile
Profiles cannot be attached to views of any kind, so the profile silently scans the source inference table instead; export the unpacked rows to CSV files and profile those files
Materialized views get no incremental processing, so each refresh re-reads everything; append the unpacked log to a Delta table with change data feed and profile that table
The profile repeats its 30-day look-back at every refresh, so the run time keeps rising; ask for a longer look-back so that each refresh covers the whole history once

stem: An inference profile is refreshing on schedule and the drift tables fill normally, but the accuracy, precision and recall columns are NULL for every window. The prediction column is configured. Which cause is most likely?

choices.text: The model was registered in Unity Catalog instead of the workspace registry, which blocks the quality metrics of an inference profile
The profile is set to a daily granularity, and quality metrics are computed only for windows of one week or longer
The drift metrics are computed first and block the quality metrics until baseline drift has been calculated for each column
No label column is configured, or the ground-truth labels were never joined to the logged predictions, so model quality cannot be calculated

stem: A data scientist created an inference profile. The risk team has no other access to the schema, but must read the profile metrics and drift metrics tables and wants to build its own SQL alerts on them. How is that access controlled?

choices.text: Access follows the profile's notification settings, so the emails listed per event type are the principals allowed to query the tables
The metric tables count as system tables that every workspace user can read automatically, so the risk team needs no grant at all to query them
The creator owns the metric tables, and the risk team gets Unity Catalog privileges such as SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA
Only the dashboard can be shared; the tables behind it cannot be granted, so the risk team needs a nightly copy of them in its own schema

stem: A customer complains that the endpoint returned a nonsensical score for one specific request yesterday. The ML engineer needs the exact input payload and response, the HTTP status code and the execution time of that single request. Which monitoring component holds that detail?

choices.text: The inference table of the endpoint, which logs request and response payloads with status codes and timing in a Unity Catalog Delta table
The aggregated profile metrics table, which stores the raw payload of every request for each time window
The Model Registry page of the model version, which keeps a copy of each scored request for 90 days
The dashboard created by the profile, which can be filtered down to one single request with the request id widget of its filter bar

stem: A regulated team must keep system logs, custom application logs, metrics and traces of a custom model serving endpoint for years, queryable with SQL. The endpoint health metrics in the Serving UI are only available for the last 14 days. Which approach meets the retention requirement?

choices.text: Take a screenshot of the Serving UI charts every week and store the images in a volume together with the audit documents
Configure OpenTelemetry telemetry on the endpoint so that logs, metrics and traces persist to Unity Catalog Delta tables for long-term retention
Keep only the ephemeral service logs, because stdout and stderr streams are stored in the logs tab of the endpoint without any time limit
Increase the granularity of the profile to one year so that the metric tables keep the endpoint logs for that period

stem: After the nightly profile refresh succeeds, business stakeholders who open the profile dashboard in the morning still see last week's charts. The metric tables already contain the new windows. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: Dashboards read the baseline table only, so the new windows appear after the baseline table is replaced by the latest data
The profile refresh also needs a manual publish of the dashboard, and only the profile owner can publish it for other users as well
The metric tables sit in another catalog than the dashboard reads, so the output schema must change
The dashboard refreshes separately from the profile, so its queries must run again after the profile refresh, for example on a schedule

stem: The on-call team wants a Slack or PagerDuty notification when the population stability index of any numeric feature of a served model exceeds an agreed threshold. The drift metrics table is refreshed daily by the profile. Which design implements this with documented features?

choices.text: Run a notebook every hour that reads the dashboard widgets and posts a message to the channel with a webhook
Add the on-call address to the profile's email notification setting, which sends a message whenever any drift metric crosses a threshold
Set the endpoint's rate limit to the threshold, so that requests are refused when the drift of the inputs is too large
Create a Databricks SQL query on the drift metrics table and an alert on it with a notification destination such as a webhook, Slack or PagerDuty

stem: A team configured email addresses in the profile's notification settings, and expected an email when feature drift increased last week. Drift was clearly visible in the drift metrics table but nobody was notified. What is the reason?

choices.text: The email limit was exceeded, because a profile sends at most one email per week for each monitored column
Emails are sent only for baseline drift, and the profile had no baseline table, so none were generated
The notification settings cover events such as a failed or timed-out refresh and never check drift values; drift needs a SQL alert on the drift table
Notifications work only for snapshot profiles, so the inference profile could not send any email about drift, whatever the thresholds in the metric tables were

stem: An inference profile covers a model with 120 features. Alerting on each feature separately would create 120 alert objects to own and tune, and a single event can shift many features together. Which design gives the team a manageable but still specific alert?

choices.text: One alert whose query returns the columns whose drift against the baseline is above the agreed threshold in the latest window, firing if any row comes back
One alert on the average of all drift values across the 120 columns, which hides a single strongly drifting feature in the mean
One alert on the number of rows in the profile metrics table, because a new window is written only when some feature has drifted
120 alerts created by script, one per feature, each with its own destination and threshold, because a query is unable to group several features together

stem: A SQL alert was built from a dashboard query on the drift metrics table, with the query parameter `:model_id` whose default is 1. After version 2 replaced version 1 in production, the alert never fires although version 2 inputs drifted. What should the team check?

choices.text: The size of the baseline table, because drift for a new model version is computed only if the baseline has at least one million rows
The default parameter value, because an alert based on a query with parameters uses the default values, so it still evaluates version 1
The refresh history of the dashboard, because alerts are evaluated only after someone opens the dashboard
The notification destination, because alerts on parameterized queries send messages only to the query owner

stem: A monitoring owner worries that the drift alert would stay silent if the profile stopped refreshing, for example after a schedule was disabled or the refresh failed repeatedly. Which design closes this gap?

choices.text: Add a freshness alert on the metric tables (latest window end older than expected) and set the profile's failure notification
Remove the profile schedule and refresh it only on demand, so that no scheduled run can fail silently
Rely on the existing drift alert, because it also evaluates to true whenever no new rows are found in the drift metrics table
Increase the alert evaluation frequency to every minute, which forces the profile to refresh when the alert notices stale data

stem: A team wants a notification when the whole-table accuracy of the production model version falls below 0.85 in any window. The inference profile has both the prediction and the label column configured. Which source and filters feed the SQL alert?

choices.text: The drift metrics table, filtered to `column_name = 'prediction'`, alerting on `avg_delta`, because model quality is the change of the average prediction
The charts of the profile dashboard, because accuracy is calculated only when the dashboard is opened and is never stored in a table
The profile metrics table filtered to the column `label`, alerting on its `avg`, because the mean of a binary label equals the accuracy
The profile metrics table with `column_name = ':table'`, `slice_key IS NULL` and the production `model_id`, alerting on `accuracy_score`

stem: The validation set of a churn model is stored in `ml.churn.validation`. It has the same feature columns as the logged table of the endpoint, but no timestamp column, and two columns have other names and types. The team wants it as the baseline of an inference profile. What is the correct handling?

choices.text: Rename and cast the columns of the logged table to the validation set's names, because a baseline cannot be a view and cannot differ in types
Create a view that renames and casts the columns to the schema of the profiled table and use that view as the baseline; the timestamp column may be absent
Use it only for a snapshot profile, because inference profiles take their reference automatically from the first window of the primary table
Add a timestamp column holding the current time to the validation set, because a baseline table is not accepted without a timestamp column in it

stem: An engineer queries the drift metrics table of a time series profile and finds only rows with `drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE'`. The team expected comparisons with the training distribution. What is missing?

choices.text: The granularity is too small, and baseline rows appear only for weekly or monthly granularities
The slicing expressions were not set, because baseline comparison is computed only for slices and not for the whole table
No baseline table was set in the profile configuration, and baseline drift is calculated only if a baseline table is provided
The profile has not been refreshed twice yet, because baseline rows are written only from the second refresh onward

stem: A retailer's traffic follows strong yearly seasonality. A time series profile with consecutive weekly drift raises false alarms every holiday week, while a baseline taken from last spring would also alarm. The team wants alerts only when holiday behavior itself changes. Which baseline fits?

choices.text: A baseline table holding the previous holiday period, so the current holiday window is compared with an acceptable seasonal distribution
A baseline table filled with synthetic uniform data, so that every real window differs from it by the same constant amount
A baseline table with the average of the entire previous year, because an average removes all seasonal influence
No baseline, and a consecutive drift alert with a higher threshold in December, which hides every other kind of change in that month as well as the holiday effect

stem: A retraining job overwrites the baseline table with the latest training data after each run, and the team notices that baseline drift stays near zero for months, even during a known upstream data change that the dashboards show clearly. What is the design flaw?

choices.text: Baseline drift is computed only at the first refresh and then frozen, so the later windows are never compared
The baseline moves with the data: a reference replaced by recent data is always the new normal, so it cannot expose changes since validation
The baseline table must be in a different catalog than the primary table, because otherwise both are read from the same cache
The baseline must have a timestamp column in its schema, because rows without timestamps are ignored by the drift calculation of the profile when it refreshes

stem: A nightly rewritten dimension table `ml.crm.customer_dim` has a snapshot profile. After a faulty load last month, the team wants drift information that shows when the distributions of the table move away from a version they consider healthy. What should they add?

choices.text: A time series profile on the load date, because snapshot profiles can never report drift of any kind against an earlier reference
A second snapshot profile on the same table, because one profile can compare only with rows added since its previous refresh and no more
Change data feed on the table, because drift metrics are written only for tables that have a change data feed enabled
A baseline table holding a copy of the table from when its distributions were acceptable, with the same schema

stem: An analyst runs `SELECT window.start, avg_delta FROM main.ml.tx_drift_metrics WHERE column_name = 'amount' AND drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE' AND slice_key IS NULL` and sees `avg_delta = -4.2` for one window. What does this value mean?

choices.text: The average amount of that window is 4.2 percent of the average in the previous window
The average amount of that window is 4.2 above the average of the baseline table
The average is 4.2 below the previous window's, as delta is current minus comparison
The model's average prediction error fell by 4.2 relative to the previous window, as quality is also stored there

stem: Two versions of a regression model (ids `7` and `8`) served in parallel are logged into one inference table with a model version column configured as the model id column. The team wants the daily RMSE trend of each version for the whole table. Which query reads it from the profile metrics table?

choices.text: Query the profile metrics table with `column_name = ':table'`, `slice_key IS NULL` and `model_id IN (7, 8)`, ordered by `window.start`
Query the profile metrics table with `log_type = 'BASELINE'` and `column_name = 'prediction'`, grouped by version, for the daily error
Query the drift metrics table, filter `column_name = 'prediction'` and plot `avg_delta`, as the change of the mean prediction measures the error
Query the profile metrics table without slice filters, and average `root_mean_squared_error` over all rows, because every row is a separate model

stem: An inference profile for a binary classifier shows accuracy, precision, recall and F1 per window, but `log_loss` and `roc_auc_score` are NULL. The label and prediction columns are configured. What is missing?

choices.text: A baseline table, because the ranking and probability metrics are computed only for BASELINE rows
A weekly granularity, because threshold-free metrics are computed only over windows of seven days or more
A column with the predicted class probabilities, because log loss and ROC AUC require `prediction_proba_col`
A slicing expression on the label, because ROC AUC is produced only for sliced data

stem: Overall accuracy of a classifier has been flat for two months, but customer support reports poor results for one sales region. How can the team find out from the existing monitoring whether quality fell for that region?

choices.text: Add the region as the model id column so each region is monitored as a separate model, which also removes the model version from the profile
Add `slicing_exprs=["region"]` to the profile so that quality metrics are computed per region, and read the slices from the metric tables
Lower the granularity to one hour, because an hourly window shows regional differences that daily windows average out
Create a second inference profile on the same table filtered to the region, because a table may have several profiles with different filters

stem: The team's inference profile uses a constant string `prod` in the model id column for every request, whatever the served version. After version 3 replaced version 2, accuracy dips for a week and recovers. The team cannot tell whether version 3 caused the dip. What should they change?

choices.text: Delete the metric tables after every promotion so that the new version starts with a clean history
Lower the granularity to five minutes so that the day of the version switch is separated from the rest of the data
Replace the profile with a snapshot profile, which keeps one record for the table after each refresh and so shows the latest version only
Populate the model id column with the model version when unpacking the log, so that the profile computes metrics for each version separately

stem: A claims model predicts five damage classes. The class `structural` is rare and business critical. An analyst reads the `:table` rows of the profile metrics table and wants the weekly F1 of the `structural` class alone, not an average over classes. Which expression returns it?

choices.text: `f1_score.macro`, because the macro value is the F1 of the class with the lowest support in each window
`accuracy_score`, because with five classes the accuracy equals the F1 of the rarest class
`f1_score.one_vs_all['structural']`, which reads the F1 of that class from the per-class map of the struct
`f1_score.weighted`, because weighting by support puts the most weight on the rare class in each window

stem: The inference table logs a `sampling_fraction` below 1 for many rows because requests were down-sampled. A trend chart of daily request counts computed with `COUNT(*)` falls whenever the fraction is lowered although real traffic is steady. How should the volume trend be computed?

choices.text: Multiply the count by the number of served models, because each model logs an equal part of the requests
Weight each logged row by `1 / sampling_fraction`, for example `SUM(1 / sampling_fraction)`, to estimate the real number of requests
Keep `COUNT(*)` and accept that sampled logs cannot show volume, because down-sampling removes the information permanently and for every row
Replace the time window by a longer one, because the sampling fraction averages out over longer windows
